title: Chapter IV

teacherSummary.text: Jane confides her admiration of Bingley; Elizabeth praises Jane's habit of seeing good in everyone. The narrator contrasts Bingley's easy temper with Darcy's cleverness and reserve, and introduces Bingley's sisters as proud.

vocabulary.context: “I would wish not to be hasty in censuring anyone; but I always speak what I think.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “censure”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The state or condition of being easy
vocabulary.context: Bingley was endeared to Darcy by the easiness, openness, ductility of his temper, though no disposition could offer a greater contrast to his own, and though with his own he never appeared dissatisfied.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “easiness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bingley was endeared to Darcy by the easiness, openness, ductility of his temper, though no disposition could offer a greater contrast to his own, and though with his own he never appeared dissatisfied.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “endear”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being open
vocabulary.context: Bingley was endeared to Darcy by the easiness, openness, ductility of his temper, though no disposition could offer a greater contrast to his own, and though with his own he never appeared dissatisfied.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “openness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To be set, or to sit, in the place of authority
vocabulary.context: His sisters were very anxious for his having an estate of his own; but though he was now established only as a tenant, Miss Bingley was by no means unwilling to preside at his table, nor was Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preside”: pre- (Latin prae, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: They were in fact very fine ladies; not deficient in good humour when they were pleased, nor in the power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conceited”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: They were in fact very fine ladies; not deficient in good humour when they were pleased, nor in the power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deficient”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + fic (Latin facere, "to make") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: No thanks to his gallantry for that.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “gallantry”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Bingley was endeared to Darcy by the easiness, openness, ductility of his temper, though no disposition could offer a greater contrast to his own, and though with his own he never appeared dissatisfied.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dissatisfy”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bingley had not been of age two years, when he was tempted by an accidental recommendation to look at Netherfield House.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “accidental”: ac- (Latin ad, "to") + -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Bingley's fortune came from trade, which the gentry viewed as less respectable than inherited land.

significance: Elizabeth prides herself on judging character—setting up her later mistakes.
discussionQuestions: Is Jane's generosity in judging people a strength or a weakness?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

items.prompt: What is Jane's habit in judging others?
Where did Bingley's family fortune come from?
How does the narrator describe Darcy's mind?
What does Elizabeth pride herself on?
In the line ““I would wish not to be hasty in censuring anyone; but I always speak what I think.””, what does “censuring” most nearly mean?
options: The quality or state of being open
The state or condition of being easy

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IV,” how does Austen show sisters and judgment? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter IV, how does Austen develop the idea of sisters and judgment? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IV develops the idea of sisters and judgment. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter IV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of sisters and judgment. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter IV suggests about sisters and judgment. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and point of view), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter IV to complicate the reader's understanding of sisters and judgment. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of sisters and judgment responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter IV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of sisters and judgment follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter IV and its treatment of sisters and judgment. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and point of view, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter IV as evidence for a larger claim about sisters and judgment in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of sisters and judgment. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “endeared” most nearly mean?

satQuestions.passage: “Did not you? I did for you. But that is one great difference between us. Compliments always take you by surprise, and me never. What could be more natural than his asking you again? He could not help seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in the room. No thanks to his gallantry for that. Well, he certainly is very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him. You have liked many a stupider person.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter IV”?
options: Injustice and the burden of silence

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “Did not you? I did for you. But that is one great difference between us. Compliments always take you by surprise, and me never. What could be more natural than his asking you again? He could not help seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in the room. No thanks to his gallantry for that. Well, he certainly is very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him. You have liked many a stupider person.”

annotationFocus.label: Point of view
annotationFocus.lookFor: who is telling the story and what that narrator can and cannot know

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is Jane's generosity in judging people a strength or a weakness? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are censuring, easiness, endeared, openness, preside. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““I would wish not to be hasty in censuring anyone; but I always speak what I think.”” Webster's says: Judgment either favorable or unfavorable. Now the word history: “censure”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “easiness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “endear”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Bingley's fortune came from trade, which the gentry viewed as less respectable than inherited land. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth prides herself on judging character—setting up her later mistakes. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to sisters and judgment.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Point of view, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “Did not you? I did for you. But that is one great difference between us. Compliments always take you by surprise, and me never. What could be more natural than his asking you again? He could not help seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in the room. No thanks to his gallantry for that. Well, he certainly is very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him. You have liked many a stupider person.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Point of view, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter IV,” how does Austen show sisters and judgment? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about sisters and judgment, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes sisters and judgment. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
